story: Yoho protects the western slopes of the Main Ranges of the Rockies, where glacial meltwater feeds waterfalls, turquoise lakes and the Kicking Horse River. High above the valley floor lies the Burgess Shale. More than 500 million years ago this land lay under a shallow sea, and the mud that settled on its floor preserved soft-bodied animals in such detail that eyes, guts and even brains can still be seen. Charles Walcott found the beds in 1909; they are among the most important fossil sites on Earth, and the reason the Canadian Rocky Mountain Parks are a World Heritage Site for their geology as well as their scenery.

The park is home to at least 224 species of birds and 58 of mammals, among them mountain goats, grizzly bears and pikas in the alpine, which is also important habitat for whitebark pine. Only four species of fish are native. Parks Canada's 2024 climate summary reports that Yoho, like the rest of Canada, is warming faster than the global average.

These are the traditional lands of the Ktunaxa and Secwépemc peoples, who hunted, fished and gathered here, and for many generations used the Kicking Horse and Amiskwi valleys as travel routes between the Columbia Valley and the plains east of the Rockies. To the Ktunaxa the park lies within ʔaknuqⱡuⱡam ʔamakʔis, the Land of the Eagle. When the park was created, Indigenous people were excluded from it and lost their ties to places within their own territories; Parks Canada now works with the Ktunaxa Nation Council and the Secwépemc Columbia Campfire Collaborative.

The railway made the park. The explorer James Hector was kicked in the chest by his horse near the pass in 1858 and named it Kicking Horse Pass; the Canadian Pacific Railway chose it for its line, and built a hotel at the foot of Mount Stephen so that heavy dining cars need not be hauled over the summit. A reserve around Mount Stephen was set aside in 1886, a year after Banff, and in 1901 it was renamed Yoho, from a Cree expression of surprise. In 1909 the Spiral Tunnels replaced the railway's steep Big Hill.
howItWorks: Every visitor who stops in Yoho needs a park pass, bought at the park gates, visitor centres, staffed campground kiosks or online. A daily pass is valid until 4 pm the day after purchase and also covers Banff, Jasper, Kootenay, Mount Revelstoke, Glacier, Waterton Lakes and Elk Island; youth aged 17 and under get in free. The Parks Canada Discovery Pass covers more than 80 Parks Canada destinations for twelve months. Admission was free during the Canada Strong Pass periods of 2025 and 2026; the last ended on 7 September 2026 and regular fees apply again.

Lake O'Hara is managed to protect a small and sensitive alpine area. Access is managed through reservations on the Parks Canada bus up the 11-kilometre road, on which cycling is prohibited: in 2026 day-use seats were allotted by random draw, with applications from 2 to 23 March, and the bus ran from 19 June to 4 October. The 30-site Lake O'Hara campground must be booked ahead, opened for 2026 on 10 February, and allows at most three nights. You may walk the road, 22 kilometres there and back, but may not camp without a reservation. The Burgess Shale beds at Walcott Quarry and Mount Stephen can be visited only on Parks Canada guided hikes, which are booked in advance.

Camping is allowed only in designated campgrounds with a camping permit and a park pass. Frontcountry sites are booked through the Parks Canada Reservation Service, which opened for 2026 on 20 January. Every overnight trip into the backcountry needs a backcountry permit, booked the same way from 26 January in 2026, with a maximum of three nights at any one campground; random camping is allowed only in designated areas, by permit, and campfires are not allowed anywhere in the backcountry. To stop the spread of whirling disease, every lake and river in Yoho and Kootenay is closed to boats, paddleboards and angling until 31 March 2027. Recreational drones are banned, with fines up to $25,000.

sightNotes.poi-ca-yoho-takakkaw-falls: Canada's second-highest waterfall, reached by a flat, paved 0.9-kilometre path at the end of Yoho Valley Road, 17 kilometres from Field. The road opens mid-June to mid-October.
sightNotes.poi-ca-yoho-emerald-lake: A green lake ringed by peaks, with a lodge and a 5.2-kilometre shoreline loop. The road from the Trans-Canada Highway is open all year.
sightNotes.poi-ca-yoho-lake-ohara: An alpine lake ringed by high routes, reached by reserved bus, an 11-kilometre walk, or a stay at the lodge, hut or campground. Best hiking July to late September.
sightNotes.poi-ca-yoho-spiral-tunnels-viewpoint: Watch trains disappear into one tunnel and emerge from another at a different height; 25 to 30 pass daily, on no fixed schedule. Closed mid-October to mid-May.
sightNotes.poi-ca-yoho-walcott-quarry: The classic Burgess Shale fossil site, open only to Parks Canada guided hikes: 24 kilometres and 900 metres of climbing from Takakkaw Falls in about 11 hours.
sightNotes.poi-ca-yoho-mount-stephen: The peak above Field, with Burgess Shale trilobite beds reached on a steep guided hike of 8 kilometres and 800 metres of climbing from the visitor centre.
sightNotes.poi-ca-yoho-wapta-falls: The widest waterfall on the Kicking Horse River: a family walk of 2.2 kilometres each way, near the park's west boundary. Its road closes late October to late May.
sightNotes.poi-ca-yoho-kicking-horse-pass-national-: The highest point on the Trans-Canada Highway, at the park's eastern edge, where the railway crossed the Great Divide and opened British Columbia to the rest of Canada by rail.

entrances: The Trans-Canada Highway (Highway 1) from Lake Louise in the east, over Kicking Horse Pass; Field is 30 kilometres from Lake Louise
The Trans-Canada Highway from Golden in the west, 58 kilometres from Field

Yoho Valley Road, 5 kilometres east of Field, to Takakkaw Falls and the Yoho Valley trailheads
planYourVisit.reservations: The Lake O'Hara day-use bus is allotted by random draw in March and the Lake O'Hara campground opens for booking in February; frontcountry campsites, backcountry campgrounds and Burgess Shale guided hikes are booked through the Parks Canada Reservation Service, online at reservation.pc.gc.ca or on 1-877-737-3783. Hoodoo Creek is first come, first served. Dates change every year — check before you go with Parks Canada.

chronology.text: James Hector of the Palliser Expedition is kicked by his horse and names Kicking Horse Pass.
A reserve is created around Mount Stephen, one year after Banff, the beginning of Yoho National Park.
The Mount Stephen reserve is renamed Yoho.
Charles Walcott discovers the Burgess Shale fossils.
The Spiral Tunnels open, replacing the steep grade of the Big Hill.
Yoho, with the Burgess Shale, becomes part of the Canadian Rocky Mountain Parks World Heritage Site.
Lake O'Hara day-use bus seats are allotted by random draw; every lake and river stays closed to boats and angling against whirling disease until 31 March 2027.

safety: Grizzly and black bears live throughout the park. Carry bear spray and know how to use it, stay alert without headphones, and keep all food and scented items in a hard-sided vehicle or food locker.
Snow can fall in any month, and high routes around Lake O'Hara and the Yoho Valley stay snowbound and may carry avalanche hazard into late June. Check trail conditions before setting out.
Mobile coverage is limited. In the backcountry carry a first-aid kit and a satellite messenger, and plan for at least a day longer than your trip.
At Takakkaw Falls and Wapta Falls stay on the path: climbing on the rocks is dangerous, and there is no maintained trail to the base of Wapta Falls.
regulations: Never feed or leave food for wildlife; all food and garbage must be stored in bear-proof containers or packed out.
Recreational drones may not take off or land in the park, with fines up to $25,000.
All lakes and rivers are closed to watercraft and angling until 31 March 2027 to stop the spread of whirling disease.
Collecting plants, antlers, fossils, rocks or any natural or historic object is illegal; the Burgess Shale beds may be visited only with a Parks Canada guide.

Camp only in designated campgrounds with a permit; fires only in park fire boxes, and none anywhere in the backcountry. Keep pets on a leash; they are not allowed on the Lake O'Hara bus or in its campground.

weather: Yoho's weather is pleasant but unpredictable. In spring and summer daytime highs average 16 to 23°C, but nights can drop below freezing, and rain, snow or hail can fall at any time of year. The roads to the high country open only in summer: Yoho Valley Road from mid-June, and at Lake O'Hara many higher routes stay snowbound, some under avalanche hazard, until late June, so July to late September is the prime hiking season. From October the park turns to winter. Winter or mud-and-snow tyres are required on the Trans-Canada Highway from 1 October to 30 April, and the highway is controlled for avalanches.
directions: The Trans-Canada Highway runs 45 kilometres through the middle of the park and is its only major road. Field, the only community inside the park, is 30 kilometres west of Lake Louise, 85 kilometres from Banff and 58 kilometres east of Golden, the nearest full-service towns. There is no public transport in the park, so most visitors drive; cars can be hired in Golden, Banff and Lake Louise. The Lake O'Hara bus leaves from its own parking lot on Highway 1 between Lake Louise and Field, and Yoho Valley Road and Emerald Lake Road branch off near Field. Mobile coverage is limited.
